[AND] Most D2C brands we work with in Jaipur sell in three places at once: their own website, Amazon and Myntra. Each marketplace files a GSTR-8 every month telling the department what it sold on your behalf, quite apart from the GSTR-1 your accountant files.

[BUT] Those two numbers rarely match. Returns, cancelled orders and a sale booked on the 31st but settled on the 2nd land in different months on each side. The portal does not ask why. It sends an ASMT-10 scrutiny notice, gives you 30 days to explain the gap, and if the reply is thin, the next letter is a demand with interest. samples.text:
[Before] It is the 3rd of the month, 9:40 pm, in a finance bay in Koramangala. Your AR executive has the bank statement open in one window and the invoice register in the other. A customer paid Rs 47,250 against an invoice of Rs 52,500, because they deducted 10% TDS and never said so. Another payment came in with a UTR and no invoice number in the narration. She is matching these one by one, in Excel, with a highlighter colour for each kind of problem, and the close cannot start until she finishes.

[After] Same 3rd of the month, 11 am. Every bank line that has an obvious invoice is already matched. The Rs 47,250 payment sits against its invoice, tagged "TDS short-payment, 10%". What is left on her screen is a short exception list, each line with the reason the system could not match it. She spends the day on those, not on the whole statement, and the close starts on time.

[Bridge] Milaan reads your bank feeds and your open invoices from Tally or Zoho Books every morning and matches them on amount, date, UTR and customer GSTIN. When your team approves a match, it learns the pattern: a customer who always deducts TDS, another who always pays in two parts. Send us last month's bank statement and invoice register, and on a 30-minute call we show you the exception list Milaan produces from it.

samples.text:
[Exordium] D2C founders in Jaipur ask us how to reply to a GST notice. The better question is how not to get one. Our position: reconcile your marketplace sales against your own returns every month, not when the notice arrives.

[Narratio] A brand reports its sales in GSTR-1. Amazon, Myntra and every other marketplace report the same sales again in GSTR-8. Returns, cancellations and month-end settlements often fall in different months on the two sides, so the figures differ. A difference can lead to an ASMT-10 scrutiny notice, with 30 days to explain it.

[Divisio] Three points. A monthly match costs less than a notice reply. Timing gaps are easy to explain while the data is fresh and hard a year later. And the comparison does not need an officer to pick you out.

[Confirmatio] First, a monthly match is a few hours of work; a notice reply means rebuilding a year [our fee and hours for each, side by side]. Second, a settlement report pulled today explains a gap in minutes; two years on, it may need a marketplace ticket. Third, both returns sit on the same portal; the mismatch shows up whether or not anyone complains.

[Confutatio] "We are too small to be noticed." Size is not the trigger; the mismatch is. A small brand with a gap gets the same notice.

[Peroratio] Match monthly, and answer the department before it asks. Send us one month's settlement reports; we'll show you your gap.

samples.brief: Framework verify (n=13): a 150-250 word piece on 'a Bengaluru B2B SaaS that automates invoice reconciliation' that follows the card's steps in order, each step labelled in square brackets.
samples.text:
Prep notes, Bengaluru reconciliation SaaS blog: "What does reconciliation software actually do?"

[Map your knowledge] Bank statement lines. Open invoices in the ERP. UTR numbers. TDS short-payments. Partial payments. One payment covering three invoices. Exceptions. Month-end close waits for all of this.

[Teach it to a 12-year-old] Think of a kirana shop that gives credit. The owner keeps a notebook of who owes money. When cash comes in, she ticks off the right name and amount. Reconciliation is that ticking, for a company. The bank statement is the cash coming in; the invoices are the notebook. The software looks at each payment and finds the invoice it belongs to, by checking the amount, the date and the reference number. When it is not sure, it puts the payment on a short list for a person to decide.

[Review and refine] Gap one: the analogy stops where the shop owner knows customers by face. A company sees only a bank reference, sometimes with no invoice number in it; say so. Gap two: "the amount" is not always equal; TDS means a Rs 52,500 invoice can be paid with Rs 47,250. Add one line on that. Gap three: does the software learn from approvals, or only follow fixed rules? Check the product documentation [link] before writing either.

[Test and archive] Explain it aloud to the new sales hire, without notes. If she can explain the short list and the TDS gap back, keep this version as the draft.

Edit pass: draft post for a Bihar district's Facebook page.

Draft: "In a truly inspiring example of community spirit and the power of digital technology, residents of a village in our district came together and successfully resolved a long-pending road issue, setting a remarkable precedent for grassroots development."

[Clear] A first-time reader cannot say which village or what was done. Name the place and use the real verb: they repaired their own road.

[Concise] Cut "truly inspiring", "the power of digital technology", "successfully" and "remarkable precedent for grassroots development". "Came together and resolved" says one thing twice.

[Compelling] Why should someone in the next block care? Give them the stake and the method. The stake: an ambulance could not reach the tola. The method they can copy: a WhatsApp group where every rupee was posted the day it was spent.

[Credible] Every claim needs a number, a name or a source. "Long-pending" becomes the month and year the road broke. Add the households, the amount, the Sundays of shramdaan, and point to the expense sheet the group already keeps.

Rewrite: "[Village], [block]: the road to the main road broke in [month, year], and an ambulance could not reach the tola. In [month], [N] households formed a WhatsApp group, pooled Rs [X], and posted every bill in it the same day. Over [N] Sundays they laid gitti and murrum themselves. The road is open again. Panchayats that want to copy the method can call ward member [name] on [number]."

samples.text:
Newsletter subject line: Jaipur CA firm to D2C founders selling on marketplaces.

Draft: "GST updates for your business". Weak on all four.

[Useful] What does the founder want? To answer a notice without it turning into a demand. "How D2C brands should answer a GST scrutiny notice."

[Urgent] There is a true clock: an ASMT-10 notice gives you 30 days to reply. Use it for founders who already have one; invent no deadline for the rest.

[Unique] Every CA newsletter says "reply on time". What only we bring is the first check we run: the marketplace's GSTR-8 against your GSTR-1, month by month. Name that.

[Ultra-specific] Add a count from our own files, or nothing: "[N] notices we answered for Jaipur D2C brands in [year]".

[Score and rewrite] Useful: strong. Urgent: strong for notice-holders, true. Unique: medium. Ultra-specific: weak until the count is filled. Rewrite the weakest first, then draft variants:

1. Got an ASMT-10? You have 30 days. Pull these 3 reports first
2. Amazon reported one number, you reported another: answering the notice
3. The GSTR-8 mismatch behind [N] of the notices we answered in [year]
4. Before you reply to that GST notice, check Myntra's GSTR-8
5. ASMT-10 reply checklist for D2C sellers (30-day window)
6. Your GSTR-1 says one thing, the marketplace says another

Pick: number 1. Useful, urgent and specific, and it reads like a colleague's note, not a sale. Hold number 3 for the next issue, once the count is checked.

Brand film for a Pune cloud kitchen's high-protein thali.

[Exposition] Neha runs a cloud kitchen in Kothrud. Her Maharashtrian thali has fed the same office crowd for years: varan, bhaji, chapati, rice.

[Rising action] Her regulars start ordering "protein bowls" from a chain instead; one tells her, kindly, that her thali is "too much rice for gym days". She builds a protein thali. The staff taste it and go quiet; it is hospital food. She reworks it with thick moong dal, soya-paneer bhurji and jowar-besan rotis, and this time the plates come back empty. Launch posters go up with the protein figure printed large. Three days before launch, the lab report arrives: the thali has less protein than the poster says.

[Climax] Late night, kitchen shut. Neha has a choice: launch on the poster's number, or pull it. She tears the posters down, moves the launch by two weeks, and sends the thali back to the lab with an extra bowl of sprouts. The second report matches.

[Falling action] The thali launches with the lab report printed on the menu, page one. A Hinjewadi gym asks to put it on their members' plan. The regular who complained orders it on day one.

[Denouement] Now nothing new goes on Neha's menu until the lab has seen it, and the report goes up next to the photo.

About page for Likho, a tool that turns Hindi voice notes into meeting minutes.

[Why] We believe the record of a decision should not depend on who in the room can type English. A lot of India's work is decided out loud: a contractor's voice note from site, a call between the sales head and a distributor, a "haan, kar dete hain" at the end of a long conversation. Then nobody writes it down, and by Friday there are three versions of what was agreed.

[How] So we built Likho for the voice note, not the keyboard. It works inside WhatsApp, so nobody on your team installs anything new. It listens to Hindi and Hinglish the way people actually speak it, accents and English words included. The minutes come back in the language your team reads, Hindi or English. Every decision gets a person's name and a date against it, because minutes without an owner are just a transcript. And we delete the audio after [X days]: your minutes stay, your voice does not.

[What] Likho turns voice notes and recorded calls into minutes on WhatsApp, for teams that already run on voice. Plans start at Rs [price] a month for a team of [N]. Forward one voice note to [Likho WhatsApp number] and read your first minutes before you decide anything else.

Customer story for a state campaign on the central rooftop-solar subsidy. [Illustrative draft: replace with a real beneficiary's account, used with consent.]

[Departure] Sushila Mishra has run her Gorakhpur household from a diary for decades, and every summer the bijli bill is the line that breaks the budget. When the rooftop-solar subsidy was announced, a neighbour's son posted the portal link in the mohalla WhatsApp group. She ignored it for months: online forms, bank details, strangers on her roof. Then the May bill came, and she handed her phone to her granddaughter Riya and said, "Woh link kholo."

[Initiation] The first installer who knocked wanted the full amount in cash. Riya checked the portal's list of registered vendors; he was not on it. They chose one who was. The DISCOM's feasibility approval took [weeks], and after the panels went up, the net meter took longer, while neighbours asked if the panels were decoration. The hardest moment came at payment: the vendor had to be paid in full before the subsidy could be claimed, and Sushila broke the fixed deposit she had kept for Riya's college. Then the inspection passed, and Rs 78,000, the scheme's fixed subsidy for a 3 kW system, arrived in her account. Riya's FD was the first thing she refilled.

[Return] Sushila now keeps a second diary, of her neighbours' applications. She has sat with [N] families on the portal, and she tells every one of them the same thing: "List mein naam nahi, toh paisa nahi."

samples.text:
Hinglish reel, 45 seconds, for a 30-day spoken-English course aimed at Tier-2 college students. Trainer to camera, in a college corridor.

[Hook] (On screen: "Tell me about yourself" in big type.) "HR ka pehla sawaal, aur aap 'Myself Rahul' bolke atak jaate ho? 3 changes, 40 second mein. Interview mein yahi line bachayegi."

[Retain] "Change 1: 'Myself Rahul' mat bolo. Bolo, 'I'm Rahul, a final-year B.Com student from Bareilly.' Name, course, city. Ek line, done." (Cut to the line on screen.) "Par asli farak change 2 mein hai."

[Retain] "Change 2: marks mat padho, wo resume mein hai. Ek cheez batao jo aapne ki: 'I ran the accounts for our college fest, with a budget of [amount].' Ek kaam, ek number." (Cut: student nodding, fest poster.) "Aur change 3 sunke aap apna poora answer badal doge."

[Retain] "Change 3: answer ko hawa mein mat chhodo. End mein bolo aap yahan kyun ho: 'I want to start in a finance team where I can learn on real accounts.' Wahan khatam karo. Smile. Silence."

[Reward] (Full answer on screen, trainer says it in one breath.) "I'm Rahul, a final-year B.Com student from Bareilly. I ran the accounts for our college fest. I want to start in a finance team where I can learn on real accounts. Bas. Itna hi. Ise 10 baar bolo, aaj raat." (Beat.) "Aise 30 answers, 30 din mein: link bio mein."

samples.brief: Framework verify (n=21): a 150-250 word piece on 'a Bengaluru B2B SaaS that automates invoice reconciliation' that follows the card's steps in order, each step labelled in square brackets.
samples.text:
Offer section, Milaan (Bengaluru invoice-reconciliation SaaS), for finance controllers.

[Dream outcome] Start your month-end close on day 2, with every customer payment already matched to its invoice, and your AR team working only on the payments that need a human.

[Perceived likelihood] Your mess is not unusual. TDS short-payments, one UTR covering three invoices, split payments: Milaan is built for these. [Two named customers in your industry: close dates before and after, with permission.] And we prove it on your data before you sign: send last month's bank statement and invoice register, and see what we matched and what we could not.

[Time delay] First result in days, not a quarter. You see last month's statement reconciled within [X working days] of sharing it. Live matching starts once Tally or Zoho Books is connected.

[Effort and sacrifice] We do the setup. Our team maps your customers, writes the first matching rules from your past data, and trains your AR lead in 45 minutes. You don't change your ERP, your bank or your approval flow, and nobody exports another Excel sheet.

[Write the offer] Rs [price] a month for up to [N] bank lines. Included: setup and rule-mapping (cuts effort), the first-month proof run on your own data (raises likelihood), a weekly exception review call for the first 60 days (cuts time). If the first full month does not cut your matching time by [agreed target], cancel and pay nothing for that month. Book the proof run: [link].

samples.brief: Framework verify (n=22): a 150-250 word piece on 'a monsoon skincare range from an Ayurvedic D2C brand' that follows the card's steps in order, each step labelled in square brackets.
samples.text:
In-house wear trial report, Ayurvedic D2C monsoon gel moisturiser. [Fill every bracket from trial data; do not round up.]

[Introduction] Customers in humid cities tell us their usual moisturiser feels heavy from June to September, so they skip it. Question: would people with oily or combination skin use an aloe-gel moisturiser (neem, manjistha, no mineral oil) daily through the monsoon, and how would it feel?

[Methods] [N] volunteers with self-reported oily or combination skin, aged [range], living in Kochi and Mumbai, used the gel twice a day from [start date] to [end date] 2026. Each filled a five-question WhatsApp form every Sunday: how oily the skin felt at 4 pm (1-5), new breakouts (yes/no), stickiness, whether they used it every day, and any irritation. A dermatologist, [name, registration number], examined every volunteer at the start and the end. Products were free; answers were not rewarded.

[Results] [X of N] used the gel on at least six days a week through the trial. Average 4 pm oiliness score: [week-1 score] at the start, [final-week score] at the end. [X] volunteers reported new breakouts in the last two weeks, against [Y] in the first two. [X] reported irritation; [X] stopped early.

[Discussion] [Interpret only after the numbers are in.] Two limits are already clear. Oiliness was self-reported, not measured, and there was no comparison group using another moisturiser. Before any pack claim, the next trial needs a comparison group and an instrument reading, and the wording goes through compliance.

samples.brief: Framework verify (n=23): a 150-250 word piece on 'a Bihar civic story: a village that fixed its own road with a WhatsApp group' that follows the card's steps in order, each step labelled in square brackets.
samples.text:
[Lead] Residents of [village] in [block], [district] district have repaired the [X km] road linking their tola to the main road with money pooled through a WhatsApp group, and asked the block office to inspect it and take over its maintenance by [date]. The road reopened to vehicles on [date].

[Body] [N] households contributed a total of Rs [X] between [month] and [month], ward member [name] said, and every payment and bill was posted in the group, "Sadak Sudhar Samiti", on the day it was made. Villagers did the work themselves over [N] Sundays, laying gitti and murrum bought from a supplier in [town] and hiring a roller for the final day.

The road had been cut since [month, year]. During that time, ambulances and the school van could not reach the tola, and residents carried patients on foot to the main road, [name], a resident, said.

The block development officer, [name], said a junior engineer would visit on [date]. [If the BDO has not replied by filing time, say so.] Two culverts near the school still need repair; villagers said that work needs an engineer, not shramdaan.

Copies of the group's expense sheet and receipts were submitted to the block office with the request.

[Tail] [Village] lies about [X km] from [block headquarters] and has [N] households, according to [source]. The WhatsApp group was started by [name], a [occupation], who had earlier used it to organise the village's Chhath ghat cleaning.

samples.brief: Framework verify (n=24): a 150-250 word piece on 'a Jaipur CA firm that handles GST notices for D2C brands' that follows the card's steps in order, each step labelled in square brackets.
samples.text:
JTBD canvas, Jaipur CA firm handling GST notices for D2C brands. [Check each line against client calls and our inbox before publishing.]

[Struggling moment] 11:30 pm, three days into the brand's biggest sale. The founder clears his inbox and finds an email from the GST portal: a scrutiny notice, a table of figures he doesn't recognise, and a 30-day clock. His accountant files monthly returns but has never answered a notice.

[Progress] "Help me answer this notice correctly, before the deadline, so I can get back to running the business without a demand order hanging over it."

[Dimensions] Functional: a reply the officer accepts, filed on time. Emotional: stop feeling that he has done something wrong. Social: no awkward explanation to his co-founder or investor.

[Current hire] Forward it to the accountant and hope. Ask a cousin who is a CA in Delhi. Google "ASMT-10 reply format". Or leave it until the reminder comes. He switches when he realises nobody around him has read his marketplace data against his returns.

[Write]
Headline: Got a GST notice in the middle of your sale? We'll take it from here.
Body: Forward the notice and your marketplace settlement reports on WhatsApp. We match your GSTR-1 against what Amazon and Myntra reported, find where the difference came from, and draft the reply for your signature. Your accountant keeps filing your monthly returns; we only handle the notice, and we tell you our fee before we start.

samples.brief: Framework verify (n=25): a 150-250 word piece on 'a Pune cloud-kitchen brand launching a high-protein thali' that follows the card's steps in order, each step labelled in square brackets.
samples.text:
Four-slide Instagram carousel for a Pune cloud kitchen's Protein Thali.

[Ki] Slide 1: Every day at 12:45, Santosh, our delivery rider, takes one Protein Thali to the same gym in Aundh. The owner signs for it at the front desk.

[Sho] Slide 2: Four months now. Same order, same note in the app: "Kam teekha. Extra dahi." In the kitchen we decided it was for a trainer bulking up, and Santosh started calling it "the bodybuilder's thali".

[Ten] Slide 3: Last Tuesday the note changed: "Aaj Aai khud lene aayegi." At 12:45 a woman in her seventies was waiting at the gym gate with a walker. After a fall last year, her physiotherapist asked her to eat more protein. She does her exercises at her son's gym every afternoon, and eats our thali at his front desk afterwards.

[Ketsu] Slide 4: She told Santosh it tastes like the varan she used to make. We built this plate for people lifting weights. She is using it to climb her own stairs again. Same thali, same order, both of them training.

Caption: Protein Thali, Rs [price], delivered in Aundh, Baner and Kothrud. "Kam teekha" is always an option; just write it in the note, like Aaji does.

samples.brief: Framework verify (n=26): a 150-250 word piece on 'an AI tool that turns Hindi voice notes into meeting minutes' that follows the card's steps in order, each step labelled in square brackets.
samples.text:
Headline strategy: Likho (Hindi voice notes to meeting minutes), for Hindi-belt small-business owners.

[Diagnose] Pull 20-30 current ads and store listings for AI meeting-notes and transcription tools from the Meta Ad Library, Google Play and LinkedIn, and mark each as claim, mechanism or identity. [Record the split here before choosing a lead.] The hypothesis to test: English meeting tools are a late-stage market, full of mechanisms like "AI joins your Zoom call and writes the notes". But our buyer's meetings are WhatsApp voice notes in Hindi, and few ads speak to him at all. Defined that way, his market may still be at stage 1 or 2.

[Stage 1: simple claim] "Hindi voice notes ko minutes mein badlo."

[Stage 2: bigger claim] "Har voice note ke minutes, [X] minute mein, WhatsApp pe hi." Number only once timed.

[Stage 3: new mechanism] "Voice note forward karo. Minutes wapas aate hain: kya decide hua, kaun karega, kab tak."

[Stage 4: better mechanism] "Jo English tools Zoom calls ke liye karte hain, Likho WhatsApp voice notes ke liye karta hai, Hinglish samajh ke."

[Stage 5: identification] "Aap type nahi karte, bolte ho. Aapka business bhi bolke chalta hai."

If the sweep confirms almost nobody sells to the voice-note owner, lead with stage 2 once the time is measured, and use the stage 3 line as the subhead so the claim explains itself. Hold stage 4 for when English tools advertise Hindi support; keep stage 5 for the brand film.

samples.brief: Framework verify (n=27): a 150-250 word piece on 'a government scheme that gives rooftop-solar subsidies to households' that follows the card's steps in order, each step labelled in square brackets.
samples.text:
Note to the family WhatsApp group, Lucknow: rooftop solar decision.

[Introduction (SCQA)] We own the house and the terrace, and summer bills have run Rs [X] to Rs [Y] a month for two years. The central rooftop-solar subsidy pays part of a system, but the vendors who called quote 5 kW, and one wanted cash. So: should we install, and what size?

[Governing thought] Install a 3 kW system this winter under the scheme, through a vendor on the portal's registered list, paid from the FD.

[Key line]
1. At 3 kW we get the full subsidy; anything bigger costs more for no extra subsidy.
2. Our house meets every condition the scheme checks.
3. The real risk is the vendor, not the scheme, and the portal's list is how we manage it.

[Support]
Under 1: the subsidy is Rs 30,000 per kW for the first 2 kW and Rs 18,000 for the third, so Rs 78,000 at 3 kW, and it stops there (pmsuryaghar.gov.in, checked [date]). Our use: [units a month, last 12 bills].
Under 2: own house, own roof, about [area] of shadow-free terrace, connection in Papa's name ([consumer number]).
Under 3: two quotes attached. [Vendor A]: on the registered list, Rs [X] for 3 kW. [Vendor B]: not on the list, cash only, so no. The subsidy comes after installation and inspection, so we pay Rs [X] from the FD first and Rs 78,000 comes back.

No objections by Sunday, and I register on Monday.

samples.brief: Framework verify (n=28): a 150-250 word piece on 'a 30-day English-speaking course for Tier-2 college students' that follows the card's steps in order, each step labelled in square brackets.
samples.text:
Two-minute talk, spoken-English trainer, Tier-2 college seminar hall, a month before placements.

[Attention] Hands up if you have ever known the answer in class and stayed quiet because it had to be said in English. (Pause.) Keep them up if it happened this week.

[Need] In [month], companies come to this campus for placements. [Confirm count with placement cell.] Every HR round will be in English. Your marks will get you into that room. The first two minutes of English decide whether you stay in it. And it is not grammar you are missing; you have studied grammar for twelve years. You have never had enough practice speaking.

[Satisfaction] Roz Bolo is 30 evenings of exactly that practice. 45 minutes a day, batches of 12, so everyone speaks in every session. A voice task on WhatsApp every night, with your trainer's reply by morning. A mock HR interview every week. "Sir, exams hain, time nahi hai." It runs at 7:30 pm, online, recorded if you miss one.

[Visualisation] Picture placement day with it. "Tell me about yourself." You have answered it four times in mock rounds; two minutes, clean, and you are looking at the interviewer, not the floor. Now picture it without. Same room, same question, the answer ready in your head, and the silence while the HR person writes something down.

[Action] Free demo class tomorrow, 5 pm, Room [X]. Sign the sheet at the door as you leave, and bring the one question you dread most.

samples.brief: Framework verify (n=29): a 150-250 word piece on 'a Bengaluru B2B SaaS that automates invoice reconciliation' that follows the card's steps in order, each step labelled in square brackets.
samples.text:
Internal positioning statement for Milaan, a Bengaluru B2B SaaS that automates invoice reconciliation, then the customer-facing line written from it.

[For target customer] For finance teams at Indian B2B companies that raise [N]+ customer invoices a month and run AR with two to five people,

[Who need] who spend the first days of every month matching bank lines to invoices by hand, while the close waits,

[Product is a category] Milaan is an invoice-reconciliation tool

[That key benefit] that matches customer payments to open invoices every morning, including TDS short-payments and split payments, and leaves your team only the exceptions, each with a reason.

[Unlike primary alternative] Unlike the Excel sheet and VLOOKUPs your AR team uses today,

[Product differentiator] Milaan learns each customer's payment pattern from the matches your team approves, so a customer who always deducts TDS stops being an exception after the first month. [Proof: share of TDS lines auto-matched in month two at pilot customers, from our logs.]

Customer-facing line, written from the statement, not pasted from it:
"Stop matching payments in Excel. Milaan does it every morning, TDS and all, and hands your team only what it can't explain."

Supporting line for the page: "Approve a match once. Milaan remembers how that customer pays."
